title: Why databases exist at all: Codd 1970 and the Relational Model
story:
Codd's A Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks appeared in Communications of the ACM in June 1970, and its opening sentence is the whole argument: future users of large data banks must be protected from having to know how the data is organized in the machine — its internal representation. He goes on to say what the goal is, precisely: the activities of users at terminals and most application programs should remain unaffected when the internal representation of data is changed.

Notice that this is a claim about who bears a cost, not about mathematics. The relational algebra is the mechanism. The purpose is to stop a change of storage layout from being a change to every program in the building.

The paper is unusually useful because it names the specific ailments rather than gesturing at complexity. Codd identifies three dependencies of the systems of his day.

Ordering dependence: programs relying on the stored order of records break when that order changes. Indexing dependence: programs written against the indices that happen to exist must change when indices are created or dropped — even though an index is a performance device with no bearing on what the data means. Access path dependence: programs that navigate a particular route through the data break when the structure of that route changes.

Read those three together and the situation they describe is clear enough to feel. An index was added to make a report faster, and unrelated programs stopped working. That is what it means for a performance decision and a correctness decision to be the same decision, and it is why a database administrator's routine optimisation was an enterprise-wide event.

The fix is to move the boundary. A program states the result it wants; the engine decides how to get it. The order of rows on disk, the set of indices, the route taken — all become the engine's business, and all become changeable without a single application being recompiled. That is physical data independence, and it is the reason the model outlasted the systems it displaced.

Four years later the model got its human interface. Chamberlin and Boyce published SEQUEL: A Structured English Query Language at the 1974 ACM SIGFIDET workshop, with the stated aim of a language for a relational system usable by people without training in mathematics or computer programming — so the relational model could be reached without its algebra or calculus notation. It was later renamed SQL. Worth keeping the motivation in view, because it explains the language's shape: the awkwardness of SQL is what a deliberate refusal to require predicate logic looks like.

And the bill arrives where you would expect. Somebody still has to decide the access path; it is simply no longer the programmer. That work moved into the engine as a query planner with cost estimates and statistics, which changed the failure mode rather than removing it. Under the old dependencies a program broke, visibly, at compile time. Under independence the program keeps working and the plan quietly becomes the wrong one — and a query that was fast last month is now slow for reasons entirely outside the program's text.

problem.name: Physical data independence
problem.shape: Programs need data that is stored in some particular arrangement, and the arrangement will change.
tell: adding an index required changing application code
the stored order of rows is load-bearing for a program's correctness
a storage migration is scheduled as a change to every consumer
a query's text says how to fetch rather than what is wanted
problem.move: Keep the boundary where Codd put it: state the result required and let the engine choose the path. Treat any place where a program depends on stored order, on which indices exist, or on a particular route through the data as a dependency to remove rather than a detail to document.
problem.invariant: What the data means and how it is stored are separable, and once separated, the storage can change without the programs changing.
problem.breaks: Independence relocates the decision rather than eliminating it. The engine now picks the access path from statistics and cost estimates, so the failure changes character: instead of a program breaking visibly when the layout changes, a working program's plan silently becomes the wrong one, and the query that was fast last month is slow for reasons nowhere in its text.

cost.time: the planner runs on every query, and diagnosing a bad plan requires understanding a component the programmer deliberately does not control
cost.space: statistics, and the indices the planner may or may not choose to use
cost.beats: navigating pointers by hand, which is predictable and fast and turns every layout change into an enterprise-wide recompilation, and hard-coding one access path per query, which gives up the planner's ability to adapt as the data's shape changes

worked.problem: What is physical data independence, and why did it outlast the systems it replaced?
worked.reasoning:
It is the property that the activities of users at terminals and most application programs remain unaffected when the internal representation of the data is changed — which is how Codd himself put the goal in June 1970, opening with the requirement that future users of large data banks must be protected from having to know how the data is organized in the machine.

I would start by stressing that this is an argument about who bears a cost, not about mathematics. The relational algebra is the mechanism; the purpose is to stop a change of storage layout from being a change to every program in the building.

What makes the paper worth reading is that it names the three specific dependencies it was written to remove. Ordering dependence: programs relying on the stored order of records break when that order changes. Indexing dependence: programs written against the indices that happen to exist must change when indices are created or dropped — even though an index is purely a performance device with no bearing on meaning. Access path dependence: programs that navigate a particular route through the data break when the structure of that route changes.

The middle one is the sharpest, and it is the one I would use to answer the question. Under indexing dependence, adding an index to speed up a report could stop unrelated programs from working. That means a performance decision and a correctness decision were the same decision, so the person tuning storage could not act without coordinating with every team that read the data. That is not an inconvenience; it is an organisational deadlock encoded in a data model.

So the fix is a boundary move: a program states the result it wants and the engine decides how to obtain it. Order on disk, which indices exist, the route taken — all become the engine's business, and all become changeable with no application recompiled.

Why it outlasted its competitors follows directly. Navigational systems were not slower or less capable; they were more tightly coupled, and coupling compounds with the number of programs. Every year of an organisation's life adds consumers of the data, so the cost of a layout change grows while the benefit of changing it stays constant. Independence is the property that keeps that cost flat, which is why it wins over time rather than at the moment of the benchmark.

The interface question is a useful supporting detail. Chamberlin and Boyce published SEQUEL at the 1974 SIGFIDET workshop with the aim of a language usable by people without training in mathematics or computer programming, so the model could be reached without its algebra or calculus notation. It was later renamed SQL — and its awkwardness makes more sense once you see it as a deliberate refusal to require predicate logic of its users.

Finally I would name the cost, since independence is usually presented as free. The access path decision did not disappear; it moved into the engine as a planner with cost estimates and statistics. That changed the failure mode rather than removing it. Under the old dependencies a program broke visibly when the layout changed. Under independence the program keeps working and the plan quietly becomes wrong, so a query that was fast last month is slow for reasons found nowhere in its text — which is why plan inspection is a skill the model's success created.

problem.practice: Find a query in your own system whose performance depends on an index, then drop the index in a scratch copy and run it again. Nothing in the query's text changes, and that is the property Codd was arguing for — along with the reason a slow query is often not a query problem at all.

beats.broke: Programs encoded how the data was physically arranged, so a change to stored order, to which indices existed, or to the route through the data broke every program that had assumed the old arrangement.
beats.fix: Separate what is wanted from how it is fetched: a program states the result it needs and the engine chooses the access path, which leaves the physical arrangement free to change.
beats.cost: The engine now chooses the path, which means a planner, cost estimates and statistics — and the failure changes from a program that breaks visibly to a plan that quietly becomes the wrong one.

interview.q: What is physical data independence, and why did it make the relational model outlast the systems it replaced?
interview.trap: Confusing it with transactional guarantees. Independence is about the boundary between logical and physical schema; atomicity and isolation are a separate concern that a navigational system could also provide.

takeaway: Codd's first sentence was that users must be protected from knowing how data is organized in the machine, and the dependency that shows why is indexing: adding an index could break unrelated programs, making performance and correctness the same decision — so independence won not by being faster but by keeping the cost of change flat as consumers multiplied, at the price of a planner whose bad choices are silent.
